title: Oregon governor criticizes federal handling of refuge standoff
text: Oregon's governor sharply criticized the federal government's handling of the occupation of a wildlife refuge by a group of armed men, saying the situation was “absolutely intolerable” and was costing the state about $100,000 a week. Governor Kate Brown, a Democrat, said federal officials had asked her to limit her public comments about the protest, which began on Jan. 2 at the remote Malheur National Wildlife Refuge, and that she did not wish to escalate the situation. “But I will say this ... The situation is absolutely intolerable and it must be must be resolved immediately. The very fabric of this community is being ripped apart,” Brown said at a news conference on Wednesday. “The residents of Harney County have been overlooked and under-served by federal officials’ response thus far.” The takeover at Malheur was the most recent flare-up in the so-called Sagebrush Rebellion, a decades-old dispute over the U.S. government's control of millions of acres of land in the West. The occupiers have said their action supports two local ranchers who returned to prison this month for setting fires that spread onto federal land. The ranchers' lawyer has said the occupiers do not speak for the family. Law enforcement officials have so far stayed away from the refuge buildings, 30 miles (48 km) south of the small town of Burns in Harney County in rural southeast Oregon, hoping to avoid a violent confrontation. One of the occupiers was arrested last week after driving a government vehicle to a local supermarket. Brown described the situation as a “spectacle of lawlessness” that must end and said she had conveyed her very grave concerns to the U.S. Department of Justice and the White House.

text: Violence broke out on Friday in the nation's capital as protesters damaged storefronts, hurled rocks and bricks at police officers and set a limousine on fire. title: Democratic lawmakers press Kushner over New York property in letter
text: A group of Democratic lawmakers wrote on Wednesday to Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law and adviser, asking whether he had ever discussed financing for a heavily indebted Kushner Companies property in Manhattan during his talks with foreign officials. The property at 666 Fifth Avenue carries a $1.15 billion mortgage due in less than two years, and lawmakers have raised concerns that it could create a conflict of interest for Kushner. Kushner ran Kushner Companies until he sold his stake to a family trust earlier this year. He serves as a senior adviser to the president and has been involved in Middle East policymaking. In their two-page letter to Kushner, the 13 Democratic lawmakers said: “We are concerned that you may be leveraging your White House position to seek financial assistance for 666 Fifth Avenue, which according to various reports has at least $1.2 billion in debt, of which more than half is owned” by Kushner Companies. A White House spokesman declined to comment on the letter and referred the matter to Kushner's lawyer, Abbe Lowell, who could not immediately be reached for comment. Special Counsel Robert Mueller, who is investigating possible collusion between Russia and Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, has questioned Kushner. It is not known whether Mueller's team is examining issues involving 666 Fifth Avenue. Trump has denied any collusion between his campaign and Moscow officials. The lawmakers' letter, led by Rep. Ted Lieu of California, asked whether Kushner has discussed the property “with any foreign nationals or entities” in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, China, Israel, France or other countries since Trump's election on Nov. 8, 2016.

title: The N.B.A.’s Fashion Runway: Stars, Styles ... and Trash?
text: The gorgeous millionaires show up in couture. Cameras are waiting for them while their fans hover on social media, hungry for glimpses of their outfits. She would not stage these N.B.A. arrivals any other way. “These are people with megamoney behind them in every possible way,” Oliphant said. “But the runway is a linoleum floor and a tunnel,” and Teamsters can be seen setting up in the background. The basketball has been decent too, though not especially competitive. The Warriors will try to extend their lead when the series resumes in Cleveland on Wednesday night. “You stress over outfits for days,” the Warriors' Stephen Curry said in an interview, “and you wind up wearing it for 30 seconds when you walk from the parking lot to the locker room.” But those 30 seconds matter.

He calls it the Freddie Gray effect.

title: Hillary Clinton’s Lead Has Narrowed: How to Read the Polls
text: The presidential race has grown much murkier over the past few weeks. At one point Hillary Clinton held a large lead over Donald J. Trump. Her lead has since slipped, but by how much is not so clear. The various forecasting models and polling averages have diverged about as much as they have all year. So what is happening? Back then Mrs. Clinton led national polling by roughly eight percentage points. Since that time, there has not been much evidence to confirm such a large margin. Yes, a few polls have shown her with a big lead. Monmouth, Quinnipiac and USA polls all had her ahead by at least seven points nationally. But note that over the past two weeks there really has not been any sign that Mrs. Clinton was ahead by, say, double digits. If she were still up by eight points, we would expect at least some data showing her with huge margins. By contrast, plenty of recent polls show a much closer race. Many of them are less reputable, including online and automated polls of questionable methodological quality or with limited or no track records. But there have been polls showing a smaller lead for Mrs. Clinton, and even the poll this week that had her down by two points among likely voters. A few weeks ago, hardly any polls of any kind showed her in such a weak position. Gallup's daily tracking poll, another measure, also showed Mrs. Clinton's favorability ratings slipping over the second half of August, which has tended to move with changes in her overall standing in national polls. Battleground state polling also points to a tighter race. Recent Marquette, Monmouth and Suffolk polls were taken in Wisconsin and Michigan.

title: The paintings 'almost no one else seemed to be doing'
text: When Judith Gait met “Father X,” it was a lopsided grief that brought them together. Years ago he had lost his only chance at fatherhood through an abortion. Gait is a married mother of five and a long-term American resident in Britain. Her support for the pro-life movement springs from “thankfulness and praise” for life and from her Christian faith. Having witnessed abortion's heavy toll on the living and the dead, Gait began creating the paintings almost no one else seemed to be doing. Subtle and working wholly through symbolism, these simple artworks refuse to scream about abortion. Instead, they mourn in color, symbol and tone, with single shoes, broken cord, dead flowers and other lonely and broken things. When a friend first visited Gait's studio, her abortion paintings struck him deeply. Confessing years of torment after his partner aborted his child, he wrote: “I realize your work comes from a place of great love, for it attempts to give defenseless life the dignity and protection it never knew in our throw away culture.” Gait invited him to pray with her for his lost child. It turned out to be the anniversary of his baby's death, five years to the day. Father X remembers every detail. Their conversation grew into a shared effort, culminating in a book, “Troubadours Sailing Hibiscus Seas: Meditations on Post Abortion Trauma.” Father X wished to remain anonymous, as a place-setter for millions of unconsidered fathers in the acts of abortion. He wrote poetic and powerful statements for each of Gait's 30 paintings in the book, which have also been shown together in art exhibits. Time and neglect do not necessarily heal the wounds of abortion, Gait claims.
